source.title: Distillability of LLM Security Logic: Predicting Attack Success Rate of Outline Filling Attack via Ranking Regression
source.authors: Tianyu Zhang; Zihang Xi; Jing-Yu Hua; Sheng Zhong

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table layout is flattened, but Table 1's model and dataset values are assignable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures harmful-response rates for outline-filling jailbreak prompts and reports attack optimization results, but does not test fine-tuning-induced safety loss, first-token concentration, compliant-opening bypasses, safety localization, the cause of shallowness, or deepening safety.
record.gate_note: The study's target-model ASR and related attack outcomes are recorded as findings about the claim's subject, but they do not measure any listed claim version. Proxy prediction accuracies and generalization scores are omitted because they measure the proxy's predictions, not target-model safety behavior.
record.test_reason: The study proposes an outline-filling jailbreak and a proxy model that ranks prompts by attack success. It measures harmful-response rates only under that decomposition attack. It has no harmful or benign fine-tuning of the target, no per-token KL, no prefill, suffix or decoding manipulation of the response opening, no parameter localization, no causal account of shallowness, and no deepening training. Qi et al. (2310.03693) is cited only as a reference for score-based ASR definitions. The record's relation 'tests' contradicts its own T6 tranche. The correct relation is cites_only.
record.authors_conclusion: The first sentence is right. The authors conclude that jailbreak success under outline-filling is a predictable, distillable property of the prompt. A Ranking Regression proxy predicts relative ASR (about 69–79%) and ALR (about 79–91%), and its rankings improve black-box attack efficiency. The second sentence of the record is the reader's gloss: the authors never discuss token depth or fine-tuning-induced safety loss.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and evaluates an outline-filling attack and ranking-regression proxy; it does not reproduce the fine-tuning or token-depth methods in the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary across target models and between the JBB and HB datasets. The study also separates ASR and ALR prediction tasks, but those proxy prediction results are not target behavior rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Outline-filling decomposition prompts elicit judged-harmful long responses from Llama-3-8B, GPT-4o-mini and Qwen. IASR is 40–69% on JBB and HB (Table 1), with QSR of 99–100%. Proxy-guided ranking raises IASR and cuts the expected number of queries to first success (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Structural decomposition (outline-filling) prompts bypass refusal in safety-trained chat models at substantial rates, and per-prompt success is predictable by a learned proxy.

record.problems: The paper does not report uncertainty estimates for the tabulated attack rates. Attack evaluation is specific to outline-filling prompts and the tested targets; the authors note that other attack types and larger target models require further validation. The Table 3 layout in the supplied text is flattened, preventing reliable per-model assignment of its entries.
record.rows_left_out: Proxy ranking accuracies in Table 2 and proxy generalization results in Table 4 were left out because they measure the proxy's predictive performance rather than target-model harmful-response behavior. Per-model Table 3 entries were not extracted because the supplied flattened layout does not reliably associate all values with their model and dataset columns.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning of target models on harmful data.
No benign fine-tuning of target models. The proxy is fine-tuned, but its safety is not measured.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL or position analysis.
Outline-filling is a prompt-decomposition attack. No prefilled compliant openings, suffixes or decoding changes are tested.
No test of data or objective causes of shallow alignment.
No deepening defense is trained or evaluated.

record.verdict_notes: There is no instruction-like content directed at the reader. Table 1 has no refusal baseline (e.g. direct harmful question), so even as an attack-rate result it lacks a no-attack comparison. Harmfulness was judged by GPT-5-nano with a strict any-of-3-unsafe vote and a 300-character length filter, which may inflate ASR.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or resulting refusal/compliance change is tested.
No fine-tuning on benign data or resulting harmful-compliance change is tested.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement is reported.
The study tests outline-filling prompts, not compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as ways to get past response-opening tokens.
No weight or rank localization/ablation of safety behavior is tested.
No data or training-objective explanation for safety shallowness is tested.
No training to deepen safety behavior or evaluation of its robustness is reported.

rows.subject: target models (aggregate; individual models not specified)
rows.operation_detail: The proxy ranks attack instructions and selects high-ranked prompts for attack optimization.
rows.note: The paper reports this aggregate outcome in its contribution summary; the table's flattened layout does not support assigning a specific value to each model.
rows.check: This is the study's own proxy-guided prompt selection compared with a random-order baseline (Table 3, top-20% selection). It is a method-performance and selection value, not a target-behaviour rate on any version. The aggregate 'over 40%' comes from the contribution summary. Table 3 per-model values exist but are irrelevant to the claim.
